newsitem.title: FRANCE: Corsican separatist leader Santoni surrenders.
newsitem.headline: Corsican separatist leader Santoni surrenders.

text.p: Francois Santoni, head of the outlawed Corsican National Liberation Front -- Historical Branch (FLNC) separatist group gave himself up on the Mediterranean island on Monday, French police told Reuters.

Santoni, who had been living as a fugitive from justice as well as in fear of rival separatist groups for months in the Corsican "maquis", the dense underbrush covering much of the island, surrendered in the northern town Bastia, police said.
Santoni's surrender came hours after police arrested his close friend, Marie-Helene Mattei, a lawyer who specialised in defending separatists before French courts.

The FLNC is held responsible by police for dozens of bomb attacks against government and other buildings on the island in the past few months. Santoni is officially head of the Cuncolta Naziunalista party, the FLNC's legal wing.
The attacks, which have cut deeply into the picturesque island's tourist trade, have caused few casualties since virtually all are carried out at night against empty premises.
Mattei was detained by police in connection with a bomb attack against a luxury golf club which investigators believe was linked to an extortion attempt by separatists.
Her detention followed that of eight other suspects in connection with Thursday's attack on the Sperone golf course.
Investigators said her arrest was a sign of the government's determination to restore order on the island after President Jacques Chirac last week said bombers would be tracked down relentlessly.
The FLNC last week threatened to step up attacks on the French mainland as part of its drive for more autonomy from Paris.
Despite being in hiding, Santoni, who was being sought by police to serve a sentence on weapons charges, appeared in a television interview on Friday, urging talks with Chirac.

Thursday's bomb flattened the golf course keeper's house but caused no injuries. The FLNC claimed responsibility for the bombing, accusing the golf course owners of letting French commandos use the building.
The owners filed a legal complaint, saying they had been asked for money in a mafia-style, cash-for-protection racket.

No one had filed such a complaint before, and investigators are hoping the case will prove a turning point in a battle against a widely rumoured "revolutionary tax" levied by guerrillas on hotel and restaurant owners.
The FLNC said in a statement last week it planned "new forms" of attacks on the mainland in its two-decade-old campaign to win greater autonomy for the island.
